summary.text: Introduce the integer sequence \(c_0=2,c_1=56\), \(c_{k+2}=-4c_{k+1}-64c_k\); direct algebra shows that \(c_k^2\) satisfies the same three-term recurrence as the odd-indexed subsequence, namely \(u_{k+3}=-48u_{k+2}+3072u_{k+1}+262144u_k\). The first three terms agree, so a three-term sliding-window induction gives \(a_{2k+1}=c_k^2\) for every \(k\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
a_{m+4}=-4a_{m+3}+256a_{m+1}+4096a_m. \tag{1}
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a perfect square.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
c_0=2,\qquad c_1=56,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+2}=-4c_{n+1}-64c_n\qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{2}
\]
We will prove the stronger identity
\[
a_{2n+1}=c_n^2\qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{3}
\]

First we derive a recurrence that advances the sequence \(a\) by even increments. We claim that for every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
a_{m+6}=-48a_{m+4}+3072a_{m+2}+262144a_m. \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, three consecutive instances of (1) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{m+4}&=-4a_{m+3}+256a_{m+1}+4096a_m, \tag{5}\\
a_{m+5}&=-4a_{m+4}+256a_{m+2}+4096a_{m+1}, \tag{6}\\
a_{m+6}&=-4a_{m+5}+256a_{m+3}+4096a_{m+2}. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting (6) into (7) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{m+6}
&=-4\bigl(-4a_{m+4}+256a_{m+2}+4096a_{m+1}\bigr)
  +256a_{m+3}+4096a_{m+2}\\
&=16a_{m+4}+3072a_{m+2}+256a_{m+3}-16384a_{m+1}. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying (5) by \(-64\) gives
\[
-64a_{m+4}=256a_{m+3}-16384a_{m+1}-262144a_m,
\]
so
\[
256a_{m+3}-16384a_{m+1}=-64a_{m+4}+262144a_m. \tag{9}
\]
Putting (9) into (8), we obtain
\[
a_{m+6}=(16-64)a_{m+4}+3072a_{m+2}+262144a_m,
\]
which is precisely (4).

Next we show that the squares of the auxiliary sequence satisfy the corresponding three-term recurrence. We claim that for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
c_{k+3}^2=-48c_{k+2}^2+3072c_{k+1}^2+262144c_k^2. \tag{10}
\]
To verify this, put
\[
x=c_k,\qquad y=c_{k+1}.
\]
By (2),
\[
c_{k+2}=-4y-64x.
\]
Applying (2) once more,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{k+3}
&=-4c_{k+2}-64c_{k+1}\\
&=-4(-4y-64x)-64y\\
&=256x-48y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
c_{k+3}^2=(256x-48y)^2
=65536x^2-24576xy+2304y^2. \tag{11}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&-48c_{k+2}^2+3072c_{k+1}^2+262144c_k^2\\
&\quad=-48(-4y-64x)^2+3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&\quad=-48\bigl(16y^2+512xy+4096x^2\bigr)
       +3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&\quad=65536x^2-24576xy+2304y^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This agrees with (11), proving (10).

We now establish (3) by induction, keeping three consecutive odd-indexed identities at once. More precisely, for each \(k\ge 0\), let \(P(k)\) be the conjunction
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2k+1}&=c_k^2, \tag{12}\\
a_{2k+3}&=c_{k+1}^2, \tag{13}\\
a_{2k+5}&=c_{k+2}^2. \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]

For the base case \(k=0\), the first two identities follow immediately from the initial values:
\[
a_1=4=2^2=c_0^2,
\]
and
\[
a_3=3136=56^2=c_1^2.
\]
For the third identity, first compute from (2)
\[
c_2=-4c_1-64c_0=-4\cdot56-64\cdot2=-352,
\]
so
\[
c_2^2=(-352)^2=123904.
\]
We compute \(a_5\) from the recurrence. First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4\cdot3136+256\cdot4+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256\cdot176+4096\cdot4\\
&=62464+45056+16384\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a_5=c_2^2\), and all three parts of \(P(0)\) hold.

Suppose now that \(P(k)\) holds for some \(k\ge 0\). We prove \(P(k+1)\). Its first assertion is
\[
a_{2(k+1)+1}=a_{2k+3}=c_{k+1}^2,
\]
which is exactly (13). Its second assertion is
\[
a_{2(k+1)+3}=a_{2k+5}=c_{k+2}^2,
\]
which is exactly (14).

It remains to prove the new third assertion
\[
a_{2(k+1)+5}=a_{2k+7}=c_{k+3}^2. \tag{15}
\]
Apply the step-by-two recurrence (4) with \(m=2k+1\). This gives
\[
a_{2k+7}=-48a_{2k+5}+3072a_{2k+3}+262144a_{2k+1}. \tag{16}
\]
Using the three induction hypotheses (12)–(14), the right-hand side becomes
\[
-48c_{k+2}^2+3072c_{k+1}^2+262144c_k^2.
\]
By identity (10), this is exactly \(c_{k+3}^2\). Hence (15) holds, completing the induction step.

Therefore \(P(k)\) holds for every nonnegative integer \(k\). In particular, its first component gives
\[
a_{2k+1}=c_k^2
\]
for every \(k\ge 0\). Since each \(c_k\) is an integer, this exhibits \(a_{2k+1}\) as the square of an integer. Thus every odd-indexed term of A113254 is a perfect square.
